title: Grade 7 Science — Fri, May 29
description: Nutrition in Plants — Day 5 of 5: Synthesis and reasoning
subject: science

questions.question: A plant is growing in a glass box with no CO₂ (all CO₂ removed). What happens to it?
options: It grows faster using more O₂
Photosynthesis stops; the plant will eventually die from starvation
It uses nitrogen instead of CO₂
It releases more CO₂
questions.explanation: CO₂ is a raw material for photosynthesis. Without it, no glucose is made. Respiration will use up existing sugars and the plant starves.

questions.question: Why do plants grow FASTER in a greenhouse enriched with CO₂ compared to outdoors?
options: Greenhouse is warmer so plants sleep less
Higher CO₂ concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis — more glucose is made
Greenhouse blocks pest attacks
Plants grow faster in enclosed spaces always
questions.explanation: CO₂ is a limiting factor for photosynthesis. Increasing CO₂ (up to a point) increases glucose production, leading to faster growth.

questions.question: A leaf starch experiment gives these results: Green region = blue-black with iodine; White region = brown. What conclusion can you draw?
options: Starch is present throughout the leaf
Only green regions with chlorophyll perform photosynthesis and make starch
White regions make more starch than green
Iodine test does not work on green leaves
questions.explanation: Only green cells have chlorophyll for photosynthesis → only green parts make starch (shown by blue-black). White parts lack chlorophyll → no photosynthesis → no starch.

questions.question: Cuscuta growing on a tomato plant takes water, minerals, AND organic food from the host. If photosynthesis rate increases in tomato, what happens to Cuscuta?
options: Cuscuta dies because there is more light
Cuscuta benefits and grows more since the host makes more organic food
Cuscuta does its own photosynthesis
Tomato kills Cuscuta with extra oxygen
questions.explanation: Cuscuta steals glucose and other organic nutrients made by the host's photosynthesis. More host photosynthesis = more available organic food = Cuscuta benefits.

questions.question: At night: (1) Photosynthesis stops (2) Respiration continues. Net effect on O₂ around a dense forest at night?
options: O₂ levels increase (photosynthesis adds more)
O₂ levels decrease (respiration consumes O₂ without photosynthesis replacing it)
O₂ levels stay exactly constant
CO₂ disappears at night
questions.explanation: During the day, photosynthesis releases MORE O₂ than respiration consumes. At night, only respiration runs — consuming O₂ and releasing CO₂.

questions.question: A farmer adds nitrogen-rich fertiliser to soil. Plants in that field grow greener. Why?
options: Nitrogen makes soil darker
Nitrogen is needed for chlorophyll production; more nitrogen → more chlorophyll → greener, healthier leaves
Fertiliser has green dye
Nitrogen replaces water need
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is a component of amino acids (proteins) including those in chlorophyll. More available nitrogen = more chlorophyll = greener leaves and better photosynthesis.

questions.question: An aquarium plant (like Elodea) produces visible bubbles in bright light but not in darkness. These bubbles are:
options: Carbon dioxide from respiration
Nitrogen from water
Oxygen from photosynthesis
Water vapour
questions.explanation: In bright light, photosynthesis rate > respiration rate. Excess O₂ produced in photosynthesis forms visible bubbles. In darkness, photosynthesis stops — no bubble production.

questions.question: Which farmer's practice makes MOST biological sense: planting legumes (beans) before wheat?
options: Legumes taste better
Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen into soil via Rhizobium bacteria — enriching soil for the following wheat crop
Beans grow faster so they warm the soil
Legumes repel wheat pests
questions.explanation: Crop rotation with legumes naturally adds nitrogen to soil. Legumes → Rhizobium bacteria → nitrogen fixation → free fertiliser for the next crop. This reduces chemical fertiliser need.

questions.question: Venus flytrap grows in a sunny habitat with nitrogen-poor, waterlogged soil. Which adaptation helps it MOST with this challenge?
options: Its red colour
Trapping and digesting insects to obtain nitrogen for protein synthesis
Its fast growth
Its deep root system
questions.explanation: The insect-trapping mechanism directly solves the nitrogen deficiency problem. Sun provides energy (photosynthesis); insects provide nitrogen. The waterlogged, acidic soil prevents normal nitrogen uptake.

questions.question: A scientist removes all decomposers from a forest ecosystem. The MOST serious long-term consequence would be:
options: Animals immediately die
Dead matter accumulates indefinitely and nutrients are locked up — plants eventually cannot grow as soil nutrients deplete
Nothing changes significantly
Photosynthesis stops immediately
questions.explanation: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead matter back into soil. Without them, essential nutrients (N, P, K) stay locked in dead organisms and soil fertility collapses over time.

questions.question: Why does cutting the phloem of a tree (ring-barking) kill the tree, even if xylem is intact?
options: Ring-barking cuts water supply
Phloem carries food from leaves to roots; without it, roots starve and die — then the whole tree dies
The tree cannot breathe after ring-barking
Ring-barking stops photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Xylem (water) runs inside; phloem (food) runs in the bark. Ring-barking removes bark → severs phloem → roots and stem below cut starve → tree dies slowly.

questions.question: In which situation would stomata most likely be CLOSED?
options: Cool, humid morning with moderate light
A hot, dry, windy afternoon when the plant is wilting
Just before sunrise when CO₂ has built up overnight
During heavy rainfall when water is plentiful
questions.explanation: Guard cells close stomata to prevent water loss during water stress (hot, dry, windy conditions). Conservation of water trumps CO₂ uptake when the plant is wilting.

questions.question: A plant is placed in an airtight container for 24 hours (with light for 12 hrs, dark for 12 hrs). Compare O₂ and CO₂ at the end vs start:
options: O₂ much higher, CO₂ much lower
O₂ and CO₂ approximately equal to start (photosynthesis and respiration roughly balance over 24 hours)
O₂ much lower, CO₂ much higher
No change at all
questions.explanation: Over 24 hours (12 light + 12 dark), daytime photosynthesis (O₂ out, CO₂ in) roughly balances the 24-hour respiration (O₂ in, CO₂ out). Net exchange ≈ zero.

questions.question: Deep-sea plants don't exist (only algae near surface). The PRIMARY reason is:
options: Sea water is too salty for plants
Sunlight cannot penetrate deep water — no light means no photosynthesis
Deep sea has too much CO₂
Fish eat all plants in deep sea
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis requires sunlight. Water absorbs and scatters light — below ~200 m, no usable light reaches. Without light, no photosynthesis, no plant survival.

questions.question: Which COMBINATION of factors would give the MAXIMUM rate of photosynthesis in a healthy leaf?
options: Low light, low CO₂, low temperature
High light intensity, optimal CO₂ levels, optimal temperature (25-30°C), adequate water
High temperature only
Night-time conditions with abundant minerals
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis rate is determined by limiting factors. Maximum rate requires: plenty of light, adequate CO₂, optimal temperature (enzymes work best at ~25-30°C), and water.
